title: Reload a long-arm stapler and staple two sheets together
instruction: Reload the long-arm stapler and staple the two sheets together. Finish with both arms at rest, clear of the stapler and the paper.
context: Refilling a stapler and then using it is an everyday office and school chore. On this long-arm stapler the staple drawer is pulled shut by its spring as soon as it is let go, so it takes one hand to hold it out and the other to lay the new strip in the right way up; only a strip fed to the nose by the follower can be driven through the paper.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. Parts are at real size. (1) A long-arm stapler, fixed (about 1.7 kg), lying along the left-right line 30 cm forward, its nose 5.5 cm left of the centre line and its long arm reaching left: a grey powder-coated steel base 6 cm wide and 1.5 cm tall from 2.5 to 33.5 cm left, widening beside the nose (from 3 to 20.5 cm left) into a flat paper rest that reaches 12 cm forward, with a black steel paper guide (6 mm tall) along the base 1.25 cm beyond the stapler's middle line and a chrome anvil under the nose; a black steel housing (the arm, 4.5 cm wide, 25 cm long) 1.4 cm above the base (the throat the paper goes into), with a slot along its near side in which the follower's red marker shows; and a black steel top arm (24 cm, 250 g) hinged at the housing's far end, sprung up 4 degrees, with a red rubber press pad near the nose: about 12 N on the pad takes it to its firing point, 3 degrees (11 mm) down; its stop is at 4.5 degrees. (2) The staple drawer, a front-loading magazine: a steel tray 22 cm long and 3 cm wide inside, with 3 mm lips and a rail along its floor (1 cm wide, 5.8 mm tall, a 45-degree roof with a 2 mm flat top), closed at the nose by a black cap with a red pull tab (1.2 x 1.6 cm, 3.2 cm tall); 60 g. It slides out of the nose to the right, up to 20 cm, against a return spring (5 N shut, 9 N fully out) and is pulled shut when let go. Inside the housing's mouth a steel strip guide clears a strip seated on the rail by 1 mm. (3) The follower (staple pusher), a 10 g steel block that straddles the rail inside the housing on its own slide, pushed toward the nose by a long spring (2.0 N at the nose, 2.5 N behind a full strip); with the stapler empty it rests at the nose. (4) A small wooden tray (6 x 12 cm) 20 cm forward and 27 cm left, with a fresh strip of 210 standard 26/6 steel staples on it (12.7 mm crown, 6 mm legs, 10.5 cm long, 6.3 g), legs down, lying along the left-right line. (5) Two A6 sheets of 80 g/m2 paper (10.5 cm forward-back, 14.8 cm across, 1.24 g each), a white printed one on a pale yellow one, lying on the paper rest out from under the head, the white one's middle 21.25 cm forward and 10.7 cm left. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Read live at the end of the trial. 1.0: the stapler loaded, the two sheets stapled together, and both arms at rest (every arm joint under 0.05 rad/s) with no part of either arm touching the drawer, the top arm, the strip, the staples or the sheets (contact force above 0.2 N); 0.5: the two sheets stapled together; 0.25: not stapled, but the stapler loaded; else 0.0. Loaded: the drawer slid shut (within 1 mm), the strip seated on the rail legs down (its middle within 1.5 mm of the rail's middle line, its crowns within 1 mm of resting on the rail, upright within 8 degrees, along the channel within 5 degrees), its front staple against the nose (within 1 mm, pressed on it with at least 0.5 N) and the follower pressing on its back (at least 0.5 N). Stapled: a staple driven through both sheets. The driver drives the front staple when the top arm is pressed 3 degrees down while the stapler is loaded (and has come back up to within 1 degree of rest since the last staple); it goes through each sheet lying flat on the base under the nose with the staple at least 2 mm inside its edges, and then holds those sheets together. Real-trial measures: loaded, open the drawer after the trial and look (strip legs down on the rail, front staple at the nose, follower behind it), or fire one test staple into scrap card, which comes out formed; stapled, lift the top sheet by a free corner and the lower one hangs from the staple; arms clear and at rest, from the video. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the drawer, the follower, the top arm, the strip and both sheets still (each moved less than 0.5 mm and turned less than 0.5 degrees over the last second).
reset_notes: Pull the drawer out, take the strip out and lay it back on its tray legs down (the drawer springs shut and the follower returns to the nose); put two fresh unstapled sheets back on the paper rest.
fidelity: Rigid-body sim (Isaac Sim, PhysX, 20 Hz), real sizes and spring forces; the stapler body is fixed. Drawer, follower and top arm are sprung joints. The strip is rigid, as a glued strip is; its two front staples are bodies of their own on its glue (1.5 g each, of 6.3 g). Driving is a rule: at 3 degrees, with a staple live at the nose and the follower behind it, the staple moves through the flat sheets and is fixed to them. Sheets: 0.5 mm stiff boards. Press force 12 N, light for a stapler.
